common_name: Black Barlow Columbine (Double Dark Spurless Granny's Bonnet)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Black Barlow seeds benefit from cold stratification, so fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification for spring germination; part of the spurless, fully double Barlow Series.

directions: Sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Black Barlow is a cultivar of the Barlow Series, the first Aquilegia vulgaris series bred with fully double, spurless flowers; its upward-facing, pompon-like blooms open in an unusual dark plum-purple so deep it reads as nearly black, held above lacy gray-green foliage in late spring to early summer. Bred originally for cut-flower production, it performs well in beds, borders, and cottage gardens and is a favorite of hummingbirds and bees despite its lack of nectar spurs. Plants are generally short-lived (2-3 years) but self-seed prolifically, and seedlings segregate somewhat in color, so gardeners wanting to maintain the true near-black form should rogue out paler offspring.

common_name: William Guiness Columbine (Magpie Columbine, Purple-and-White Bicolor Granny's Bonnet)

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; columbine seeds benefit from cold stratification, so fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification for spring germination; also sold as Aquilegia vulgaris 'Magpie'.

directions: Sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade. William Guiness (also marketed as 'Magpie') is a striking bicolor columbine with large, nodding flowers in near-black deep purple with contrasting white on the upper half of the sepals and short, incurved dark spurs, held above ferny green foliage from late spring into early summer. It is a bushy, clump-forming, short-lived perennial that self-seeds readily; open-pollinated seedlings vary somewhat in the depth of purple and amount of white, so gardeners wanting to preserve the classic bicolor form should divide named clumps or rogue out off-type seedlings. Popular in cottage gardens and pollinator plantings, it attracts bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; columbine seeds benefit from cold stratification, so fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification for spring germination.

directions: Sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade. Crimson Star is a classic long-spurred columbine bearing bright crimson-red flowers with a contrasting white corolla, the narrow, slightly twisted red outer petals and spurs framing the white center; blooms are held above a compact mound of fern-like, light green foliage for 4-6 weeks in late spring to early summer. It is short-lived but self-seeds prolifically, forming colonies over time, and its 4-inch flowers make excellent cut flowers. It attracts hummingbirds and butterflies while being largely ignored by deer and rabbits, making it a reliable choice for beds, borders, and cottage gardens.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; columbine seeds benefit from cold stratification, so fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification for spring germination; part of the compact, upward-facing Songbird Series.

directions: Sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Songbird Bluebird is a compact member of the Songbird Series bred for large, long-spurred, blue-and-white bicolor flowers up to 3 inches long that face upward rather than nodding, making the blooms easy to view without bending down; flowers appear above blue-green fern-like foliage for 4-6 weeks in late spring to early summer. It is a short-lived perennial that self-seeds without becoming weedy, and it attracts hummingbirds and butterflies. Well suited to containers, borders, and cottage gardens where its compact, tidy habit is an asset over taller, floppier columbine types.

common_name: Winky Double Blue-and-White Columbine (Dwarf Double-Flowered Compact Columbine)
scientific_name: Aquilegia vulgaris 'Winky Double Blue and White'

planting.note: Direct sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; columbine seeds benefit from cold stratification, so fall sowing outdoors provides natural stratification for spring germination; part of the dwarf, mildew-resistant Winky Series.

directions: Sow in fall or very early spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Winky Double Blue and White is a dwarf columbine bearing unique double, upward-facing flowers in dark blue-purple and white, blooming profusely in large bouquets for 4-6 weeks from late spring into early summer on compact plants only 12-14 inches tall and wide, making it well suited to containers and the front of borders where taller columbines would flop. The Winky Series is noted for abundant bloom, a tidy compact habit, and good mildew resistance compared to older columbine types. It is shade tolerant, attracts butterflies and hummingbirds, and is generally avoided by deer.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, well-drained, average to rich soil in full sun; Herbstsonne (German for 'autumn sun') is a tall, RHS Award of Garden Merit-winning selection of cutleaf coneflower, also sold as 'Autumn Sun'.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in moist, well-drained, average to rich soil in full sun; tolerates light shade and more moisture than most Rudbeckia. Herbstsonne is an upright, rhizomatous, clump-forming cultivar that typically reaches 4-7 feet tall, bearing large 4-5 inch daisy-like flowers with broad, drooping, bright golden-yellow petals surrounding a prominent pale green conical center that browns with age. It blooms profusely from midsummer into fall atop sturdy stems above glossy mid-green foliage, and its height and vigor make it a striking back-of-border or naturalized-planting plant that rarely needs staking. It is moderately deer- and drought-resistant and won the RHS Award of Garden Merit in 2002; leaving spent flower heads standing provides winter seed for goldfinches.

common_name: Red Satin Coreopsis (Sterile Wine-Red Threadleaf Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Red Satin is the first member of the Permathread series, bred by Darrell Probst for sterile flowers and improved hardiness in a red-flowered coreopsis.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Red Satin forms a tight clump of deep green, threadleaf foliage and produces masses of large, satiny wine-red to ruby-red flowers about 1.5 inches across with contrasting golden centers from early through late summer. Because its flowers are sterile, it does not set seed and rebloom is prolonged rather than diverted into seed production, and it will not self-seed into unwanted areas. It is notably hardier and more disease-resistant than older red-flowered coreopsis cultivars, tolerates poor, sandy, or rocky soils, and is both drought- and deer-tolerant, making it a reliable, low-maintenance choice for borders and cut-flower gardens.

common_name: Sienna Sunset Coreopsis (Apricot-to-Salmon Fading Threadleaf Tickseed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun; Sienna Sunset is a sport of Coreopsis 'Creme Brulee' selected for its warm apricot-and-burnt-sienna flower color.

directions: Plant in well-drained, lean to average soil in full sun. Sienna Sunset is an open, mounded perennial with ferny emerald-green foliage that blooms profusely from early through late summer, its large daisy-like flowers opening in warm apricot overlaid with burnt sienna before fading to a rich salmon as they age, giving a multi-toned display across the plant. A sport of the popular 'Creme Brulee', it stays fresh-looking and disease-free all season and provides strong color impact in beds and containers. It thrives in poor, sandy, or rocky soils, tolerates drought and deer browsing, and benefits from a midsummer shearing after the first flush of bloom to encourage continued flowering.
